blocks.title: Why Human-in-the-loop Agents matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A healthcare intake agent drafts answers but escalates risky medical and billing decisions to staff. The learner's job is not to memorize Human-in-the-loop Agents; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved correct escalation rate.

Running case: human-review routing policy with approval and override paths. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: Human-in-the-loop Agents matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Human-in-the-loop Agents matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure correct escalation rate on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: human-review routing policy with approval and override paths

spans.text: Scenario: A healthcare intake agent drafts answers but escalates risky medical and billing decisions to staff. The team wants to improve correct escalation rate, but it has already seen this failure: the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Request: "A returning customer asks about a refund and mentions that they prefer email updates." The agent may remember the communication preference, but it must not store payment fragments, one-time codes, or raw complaint text longer than needed.

Artifact: human-review routing policy with approval and override paths. It contains a memory schema, a write filter, retrieval rules, an escalation rule, and a tiny acceptance test tied to correct escalation rate.

Worked output: store {customer_id, preference: "email updates", source: "support chat", expires_at: "90 days"}; reject {card digits, passwords, medical details}; retrieve only when the current task is about support follow-up.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: agent designer. Context: A healthcare intake agent drafts answers but escalates risky medical and billing decisions to staff. Task: design human-review routing policy with approval and override paths. Include memory or state fields, tool permissions, retrieval rules, human review points, audit logs, and failure tests. Output: {state, allowed_actions, blocked_actions, checks, metric}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Human-in-the-loop Agents to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the mechanism in the running case

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind Human-in-the-loop Agents. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means tracking what the agent observes, remembers, decides, acts on, and writes back to state.
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

spans.text: Recall from module 1: the artifact is human-review routing policy with approval and override paths. Which single field, trace, or test would show whether correct escalation rate improved?

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to human-review routing policy with approval and override paths: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: correct escalation rate becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Human-in-the-loop Agents design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

spans.text: This is where Human-in-the-loop Agents becomes a decision. The team must choose how much rigor human-review routing policy with approval and override paths needs before it can be trusted.

The wrong move is to jump straight to the fanciest option. The useful move is to ask which option improves correct escalation rate while making this failure visible: the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: The agent remembers the wrong thing, forgets the important thing, or cannot distinguish user preference from sensitive data.
A tool call succeeds technically but changes real-world state without review.
The loop repeats because state was not updated after the last action.
The broad warning sign: correct escalation rate gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.useWhen: Use the production path when correct escalation rate affects users, trust, safety, cost, or compliance.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Make the failure visible before making the system more sophisticated.

blocks.title: Tiny implementation sketch: make the contract concrete

spans.text: A useful implementation sketch for Human-in-the-loop Agents should be small enough to inspect and real enough to fail. That means it needs a realistic input, an explicit decision boundary, and a visible output.

For human-review routing policy with approval and override paths, the sketch should prove one thing: the system can improve correct escalation rate without hiding the failure where the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action.
Predict before the code: should the system answer, retrieve more evidence, block, escalate, or mark the case inconclusive when this failure appears?

blocks.title: Runnable check: filter memory before writing it
blocks.code:
# Humanintheloop Agents: memory write gate for the running case.
items = [
    {"kind": "preference", "text": "prefers email updates"},
    {"kind": "secret", "text": "card ends in 4242"},
    {"kind": "task_fact", "text": "refund requested for invoice INV-19"},
]
allowed = {"preference", "task_fact"}

def memory_write_candidates(items):
    return [item for item in items if item["kind"] in allowed]

kept = memory_write_candidates(items)
print([item["kind"] for item in kept])
print("safe to write" if len(kept) == 2 else "review")

spans.text: This is a runnable miniature, not the whole production system. It makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision rule, output, and a check related to the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the list of kept item kinds and the final decision.
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
['preference', 'task_fact']
safe to write

The secret is filtered out before memory write. The point is not this tiny classifier; it is the boundary: memory should have an explicit write policy.

blocks.title: Verify AI-generated work before trusting it

spans.text: If an AI assistant drafts code, a prompt, a workflow, or a policy for Human-in-the-loop Agents, review it against the running case before accepting it.

items.text: Does it name the real artifact: human-review routing policy with approval and override paths?
Does it include a realistic input and a concrete expected output?
Does it test or block the known failure: the agent treats a judgment call as an automatic action?
Does it expose enough evidence to debug correct escalation rate?
Does it define what happens when evidence is missing: retry, refuse, ask a human, roll back, or mark the case inconclusive?
